In that case the second loop never runs and the method sets `p := a.Length-1`, which is less than x. So the postcondition `x<=p<a.Length` cannot hold on the final return path. With `p := a.Length-1`, the postcondition needs `x <= a.Length-1`, i.e. `x < a.Length`. The precondition is too weak to provide that.

The method has no precondition on x. The first loop starts with i:=1, so the invariant 0<=i<=x fails on entry when x==0. When x>a.Length, the invariants and the body index a[j] and a[i] out of range. The second loop's invariant x<=i<=a.Length also fails on entry when x>a.Length. The postconditions need x>=1 (the exists clause over 0<=i<x) and x<a.Length (so p=a.Length-1 satisfies x<=p). The missing precondition bounding x is the root cause of all five errors.

The predicate sorted_seg has a precondition that is too weak to make its body well-formed. The clause `j+1 <= a.Length + 1` only gives j <= a.Length. The body reads a[k] for k up to j, so it needs j < a.Length. Dafny's counterexamples show this: with a.Length = 0, i = 0, j = 0 (or a.Length = 1, i = 0, j = 1), the quantifier reaches a[j], which is out of range. Both reported errors (a[l] and a[k] at line 6) come from this. Every call site already satisfies the stronger bound j+1 <= a.Length: sorted_seg(a,0,a.Length-1), sorted_seg(a,0,i-1) with i <= a.Length, and sorted_seg(a,j+1,i) with i < a.Length in the outer loop body. So tightening the precondition fixes well-formedness without breaking any caller.

PrimeMap is marked {:autocontracts}, so InsertPrime implicitly has 'ensures Valid()'. Valid() states that every key i in database maps to true exactly when prime(i) holds. InsertPrime sets database[n] := true for any nat n, yet nothing in its contract says n is prime. With n = 4 (the counterexample), database[4] == true but prime(4) is false, so Valid() fails on return. The method's comment says it inserts 'an already known prime number', but that assumption is never stated as a precondition. As a result, the entry state does not imply the implicit Valid() postcondition.

In LinearSearch3 the precondition `requires |s1| <= (data.Length) + 1` is off by one. It allows |s1| == data.Length + 1. The counterexamples confirm this (data.Length = 0, |s1| = 1, and data.Length = 1236, |s1| = 1237). In that case the second requires indexes data[data.Length-1-i] at index -1 when i = data.Length, which is the well-formedness error at line 75. The same bound makes data[data.Length - n1 + n] in the loop index -1 at n = 0, since n1 = |s1| = data.Length + 1. The other index assertions in the body fail for the same reason, and the later `assert |s1| <= data.Length` cannot be proved. The precondition is too weak to make the loop's array accesses and its reasoning about s1 well-defined from loop entry onward.

The trait OddListSpec declares `at` with `requires 0 <= index < (|s|) + 1`, which allows index == |s|. That index is out of bounds for s. The class override OddList.at uses the stronger `requires 0 <= index < |s|`, which it needs so that `return s[index]` and its `ensures s[index] == x` are well-formed. An override may only weaken a precondition, never strengthen it, so Dafny reports at line 214 that the method must provide an equal or more permissive precondition than its parent trait. The off-by-one `+ 1` in the trait's precondition is the bug: no implementation could safely read s[|s|].

ComputeFact2 has no precondition. Its postcondition calls factorial(n), whose precondition n >= 0 cannot be proved (line 48). For n = -1, x = 0 makes the invariant 0 <= x <= n false at loop entry (line 53). The missing requires n >= 0 is needed both for the postcondition to be well-formed and for the invariant to hold on entry.

Push's precondition is only Valid(), which permits top == capacity - 1, meaning the stack is full. The body increments top and then writes arr[top]. When the stack is full, top becomes capacity == arr.Length, so the write at line 71 is out of bounds. The counterexample shows exactly this: capacity = 1 and top = 0 give top = 1 after the increment. The comment says Push is for a non-full stack, but the requires clause omits the !Full() condition. Main always calls Push on non-full stacks, so it still verifies with the stronger precondition.

The outer loop starts with i := 1, so the invariant `i <= a.Length` (line 27) requires a.Length >= 1 on entry. The precondition `requires a.Length > -1` is trivially true and allows an empty array. With a.Length = 0 and i = 1, the invariant fails at loop entry, which is exactly the counterexample. The same bound is also needed for `sorted_between(a, 0, i)` to be well-formed. The precondition is too weak to establish the invariant at initiation.

SkipHead has no precondition. Without Valid() on entry, the ensures clause has nothing to work with. The slice List[1..] may be out of range because |List| could be 0. The returned r == next is not known to be Valid(), and its List and Repr are not tied to this node's List and Repr. The method also cannot show that r == null implies |List| == 1. The missing 'requires Valid()' clause is what should supply all of these facts.

The range precondition was weakened to allow -1 <= a[i], which contradicts its own comment that elements lie in [0..a.Length-2]. Inside the loop body, the access d[a[i]] needs 0 <= a[i] < d.Length. When a[i] == -1 (the counterexample has a[3089] = -1), that index is out of range. So the loop iteration cannot be verified as safe. The lower bound must be 0, not -1.
pred_repair: requires forall i :: 0 <= i < a.Length ==> 0 <= a[i] < a.Length - 2;  // the elements of "a" in the range [0.. a.Length-2]

pred_diagnosis: The precondition of bits_trim_front is 'requires n > -1'. For a nat this is always true, so it excludes nothing. When n == 0, bits(0) == [], so the slice bits(n)[1..] in the ensures clause has its lower bound out of range. That is the well-formedness error at line 44. The postcondition then cannot be proved for n = 0, which matches the counterexample. The intended precondition is n > 0. Under it, bits(n) == [n%2==1] + bits(n/2), so bits(n)[1..] == bits(n/2) and from_bits of it equals n/2.

The function gcd only requires m > 0, so n may be 0. Its default termination measure is the lexicographic pair (m, n). With m = 1 and n = 0 (the counterexample), the branch m > n makes the recursive call gcd(m - n, n) = gcd(1, 0). Neither argument decreases, so the recursion never ends and Dafny cannot prove termination at line 55. The precondition is too weak: gcd is only meaningful and terminating when both arguments are positive.

maxArrayReverse has the precondition 'requires arr.Length > -1'. This only says arr.Length >= 0, so an empty array is allowed. With arr.Length == 0, ind becomes -1 and the access arr[ind] at line 87 (max := arr[ind]) is out of range, as the counterexample shows. The postcondition 'exists x :: 0 <= x < arr.Length && arr[x] == max' also cannot hold for an empty array. The precondition must require a non-empty array, as maxArray does.

maxArrayReverse has no precondition that the array is nonempty, unlike maxArray, which has 'requires arr.Length > 0'. When arr.Length == 0, ind is set to -1, so the access arr[ind] at line 86 ('max := arr[ind];') is out of range. The existential postcondition also cannot hold for an empty array. The missing precondition means the state before the loop cannot be set up safely.

Set.add (line 59) is missing the precondition 'requires RepInv()'. The clause 'requires size() < maxSize()' calls the functions size() and maxSize(), and both require RepInv(). With nothing on entry establishing RepInv(), the precondition is not well-formed, so the verifier reports the function precondition failure at line 59. The counterexample shows exactly this: this !in Repr, store.Length = 0, nelems = -1. The PositiveSet and GrowingSet versions include 'requires RepInv()' first and do not fail.

The precondition of query has an off-by-one weakening: it allows j <= a.Length + 1, but sum requires j <= a.Length. With j = a.Length + 1, the ensures clause sum(a, i, j) is ill-formed. The invariant's sum calls fall outside sum's domain for the same reason, and the loop body reads a[ind] with ind = a.Length, which is out of range. The precondition is too weak to make the postcondition well-defined and to support the loop.

queryFast only requires is_prefix_sum_for(a, c). It never constrains i and j. So the postcondition r == sum(a, i, j) at line 36 is not well-formed, because sum needs 0 <= i <= j <= a.Length. The call proof(a, 0, j, k) with k == i also cannot meet its precondition 0 <= 0 <= k <= j <= a.Length. The counterexamples show this: i = -1, j = 7719 > a.Length, and j < i. With bounds on i and j, three things follow: c[i] and c[j] are in range (c.Length == a.Length + 1), the lemma's precondition holds, and its result sum(a,0,i) + sum(a,i,j) == sum(a,0,j) together with the prefix-sum facts c[i] == sum(a,0,i) and c[j] == sum(a,0,j) gives r == sum(a,i,j).

The error at line 91 is in the body of predicate `merged`, at the slice `b[start..end]`. The predicate's only precondition is `end - start == |a2| + |a1|`. That says nothing about where `start` and `end` lie relative to the array. The counterexamples show this: start = -1 makes the lower bound out of range, and b.Length = 0 with end = 2 makes the upper bound exceed the array length. Dafny checks the predicate's well-formedness on its own, using only its `requires` clauses. Callers already have these bounds (the merge invariant gives start <= k <= end, and the method preconditions bound end). The fix is to strengthen the predicate's precondition with the array-bounds conditions, conjoined with the existing length condition. The existing length condition must stay, because the `ensures merged(...)` call and the loop invariant rely on it.
pred_repair: requires 0 <= start <= end <= b.Length && end - start == |a2| + |a1|

pred_diagnosis: lemma_palindromic_radius_contains passes the interval [c-r, c+r+1] to lemma_palindromic_contains and asks for the inner interval [c-r', c+r'+1]. That call requires lo <= lo', i.e. c-r <= c-r', which means r' <= r. The lemma's precondition was weakened to 0 <= r' <= r + 1. This allows r' = r + 1, for example r = 1 and r' = 2, giving an interval larger than the known palindrome. So the callee's precondition 0 <= lo <= lo' cannot be proved, and the claim itself is false in that case. Every caller only needs r' <= r: lemma_end_of_expansion uses r' > r as the outer radius with r+1 as the inner one, and lemma_mirrored_palindrome uses distances within r.

The static method substring calls split(n, i) at line 318. split requires n.Valid() (line 224). Unlike delete, substring has no precondition that n is a valid rope. Its only requires clause bounds i and j. At the call site nothing is known about n's Repr or its children, so Dafny cannot prove any conjunct of Valid(): left in Repr, left.Repr < Repr, right in Repr, Repr == {this}, and so on. The counterexample shows this: n.weight = 1 with |n.data| = 2 and |n.Contents| = 18912 is an arbitrary, inconsistent rope. The postcondition of lemma knowerCannotBeCelebrity calls isCelebrity(n, i), and isCelebrity requires 0 <= i < n. The lemma's precondition only states n >= 0 and never bounds i. So the ensures clause is not well-formed: Dafny cannot prove the function precondition when i is negative (i = -1) or when i >= n (i = 8956, n = 1237). The lemma powerLemma has only 'requires n > 0.0'. Its ensures clause calls power(n, alpha) and power(n+1.0, alpha), and power requires both n > 0.0 and alpha > 0.0. Because nothing constrains alpha, the postcondition is not well-formed: alpha could be 0, as the counterexample shows, so the function precondition 'alpha > 0.0' cannot be proved. The callers (test2 with alpha = 4.0, and pow, which requires alpha > 0.0) already satisfy the stronger precondition, so strengthening it breaks nothing.

cowspec only requires nomultiples(u). It is missing the length-equality condition that bullspec has. Its body calls recccow(s, u, 0), which requires 0 <= 0 <= |s| == |u|. Nothing guarantees |s| == |u| (counterexample: |s| = 1, |u| = 2), so the function precondition of recccow fails in cowspec's body. The precondition of cowspec is too weak to support the call to the recursive specification function.

The precondition of Exchanger bounds x by x < |s| + 1, which allows x == |s|. With that value, the postcondition t[x] == s[y] && s[x] == t[y] (line 10) indexes s and t out of range. The body update t[x := s[y]] (line 14) is also out of range when x == |s|. The counterexamples confirm this: x == |s| == 10158 and x == |s| == 571. The bound should be x < |s|, matching the bound on y.

The lemma MutualExclusion requires only `p in P` and omits `q in P`. As a result, `cs[q]` in the second requires clause is not well-formed, because q may not be in cs.Keys (== P). That is the 'element might not be in domain' error. Even apart from well-formedness, Valid()'s uniqueness and serving facts only constrain processes in P. Without `q in P`, the preconditions cannot establish that t[q] == serving == t[p], so they do not imply `p == q`. The counterexample shows exactly this: q lies outside P, so its state and ticket are unconstrained.
pred_repair: requires Valid() && p in P && q in P

pred_diagnosis: The precondition of BinarySearch was weakened to `intSeq[i] <= intSeq[j] + 1`, so the sequence is no longer required to be sorted. The counterexample shows this: intSeq[975] = 449 and intSeq[976] = 448 with key = 449. Because adjacent elements may decrease, setting `lo := mid + 1` after seeing `intSeq[mid] < key` does not ensure that every element below the new lo is less than key. Likewise, setting `hi := mid` after seeing `intSeq[mid] > key` does not ensure that every element from mid onward is greater than key. As a result, neither invariant (lines 11 and 12) can be shown to be maintained. The precondition must require a genuinely sorted sequence, as the other lemmas do.
pred_repair: requires forall i,j | 0 <= i <= j < |intSeq| :: intSeq[i] <= intSeq[j]

pred_diagnosis: The function sum's precondition bounds X_crd[i] only for 0 <= i < X_crd.Length - 1, so it skips the last index. When b == X_crd.Length - 1 and k == X_val.Length, the body evaluates v[X_crd[b]] with no guarantee that X_crd[b] < v.Length. pred_diagnosis: The invariant only bounds m and n. It does not say that key is still in the unsearched region (rows m.., columns ..n). So when a[m,n] < key the verifier cannot rule out m+1 == a.Length0, and when a[m,n] > key it cannot rule out n-1 < 0. That is why both conjuncts 0<=m<a.Length0 and 0<=n<a.Length1 fail to be maintained. The missing fact is that the eliminated row or column cannot contain key. If a[m,n] < key, every a[m,j] with j<=n is at most a[m,n] < key, so key lies in a row after m. If a[m,n] > key, every a[i,n] with i>=m is at least a[m,n] > key, so key lies in a column before n. With that fact the indices provably stay in bounds. It holds on entry from the existence precondition, since m=0 and n=a.Length1-1 cover the whole array.

In mfirstMaximum the invariant meant to track the strict 'first maximum' property was weakened to `v[i] > (v[k]) - 1`. Over integers this is the same as `v[i] >= v[k]`. At loop exit Dafny knows only the invariants and `j >= v.Length`, so it cannot derive the postcondition `forall l :: 0<=l<i ==> v[i] > v[l]`, which needs strict inequality for indices before i. The counterexample shows equal values at several indices. The strict invariant is still maintainable: i changes only when v[j] > v[i], and v[i] >= v[k] for all k < j, so the new v[i] = v[j] is strictly greater than every earlier element.

In mlastMaximum the loop invariant that bounds i (0<=i<v.Length) is missing, although mmaximum2 has it. Because the loop assigns i, Dafny knows nothing about i at the loop head except what the invariants state. So the invariants that index v[i] are not well-formed, which gives the index-out-of-range errors at lines 69, 70 and 72. For the same reason, after the loop (invariants && j<0) Dafny cannot conclude the postcondition 0<=i<v.Length. The bound on i holds on entry (i = v.Length-1) and is preserved, since i is set either to j in [0, v.Length-1) or left unchanged. It just needs to be stated, and placed before the invariants that index v[i].

The loop invariant `0<=j<=(i)+1` gives the wrong upper bound. On exit Dafny knows only `!(j<i)` together with `j<=i+1`, so `j` could be `i+1` rather than `i`. Then the invariants `s==Sum(v,k,j+1)` and `0<=k<=j` say nothing about `Sum(v,k,i+1)` or `k<=i`, and `SumMaxToRight(v,j,s)` is not `SumMaxToRight(v,i,s)`, so all three postcondition conjuncts fail. The loose bound also lets `j+1` exceed `v.Length` and `j` reach `v.Length`. That makes `Sum(v,k,j+1)` and `SumMaxToRight(v,j,s)` ill-formed inside the invariants (the function precondition errors at lines 29 and 30). The body only runs while `j<i` and sets `j:=j+1`, so `j<=i` is preserved. With that bound the exit condition gives `j==i`.

The failing invariant is the outer loop's 'forall i | i in m.Keys - keys :: multiset(s)[i] == m[i]' (line 189). To preserve it after 'keys := keys - {key}', Dafny must know that multiset(s)[key] == m[key] when the inner loop exits. The inner loop's bound invariant is '0 <= counter <= m[key] + 1'. Combined with the exit condition '!(counter < m[key])', this only gives m[key] <= counter <= m[key] + 1, so counter (and hence multiset(s)[key]) may be m[key] + 1. The upper bound is too loose for the exit condition to pin counter to m[key]. Since counter starts at 0 and grows by 1 only while counter < m[key], the tight bound counter <= m[key] holds on entry and is preserved.

The outer invariant at line 9 says rows 0..m-1 of dst already hold old(src) values. The inner loop writes dst[m,n], so dst is one of its loop targets. Its invariants only describe src and the current row m. After the inner loop, Dafny therefore knows nothing about dst rows i < m, which may have been overwritten. When m is incremented, the outer invariant cannot be re-established for the earlier rows.
pred_repair: invariant forall i, j :: 0 <= i < m && 0 <= j < src.Length1 ==> dst[i,j] == old(src[i,j])  // add this to the inner while loop's invariants

pred_diagnosis: The loop in Search2PowLoop has an invariant for the right part of the segment (elements at k+c and beyond are >= x) but none for the left part. After the loop, Dafny knows only the invariants and c == 0. Nothing tells it that elements in [i, k) are < x, so the postcondition 'forall r | i <= r < k :: a[r] < x' cannot be derived. The missing invariant does hold: when k becomes k+c+1 it is because a[k+c] < x, and sortedness then makes every element up to k+c smaller than x.
pred_repair: invariant forall r | i <= r < k :: a[r] < x;

pred_diagnosis: The loop in isSubstring has only the invariant `i >= -1`. When the loop exits and the method reaches `return false` at line 76, Dafny knows nothing about which start positions were already checked. So it cannot conclude that no j with 0 <= j <= |str| satisfies isPrefixPred(sub, str[j..]), and therefore cannot prove `!isSubstringPred(sub, str)`. The invariant must record that every position above i has been ruled out. This holds on entry: for j > |str| - |sub|, str[j..] is shorter than sub, so isPrefixPred is false. It is maintained because each failed isPrefix call rules out position i. At exit i == -1, so the invariant covers every start position and gives the postcondition.

pred_diagnosis: The invariant at line 100 fails to be preserved. The body sets arr[i] := arr[i + 1], so preserving it needs arr[i + 1] == old(arr[i + 1]). That fact should come from the 'untouched suffix' invariant, but that invariant only covers indices j < capacity - 1. It never records that the last element arr[capacity - 1] is unchanged. Since the loop may write arr, Dafny loses that fact after the first havoc. In the final iteration (i = capacity - 2), arr[i + 1] = arr[capacity - 1] is unconstrained, so arr[i] == old(arr[i + 1]) cannot be shown. The counterexample matches this: arr[177] in a 178-element array. The fix is to extend the untouched-suffix invariant to the whole remaining range up to capacity.
pred_repair: invariant forall j : int :: i <= j < capacity ==> arr[j] == old(arr[j]);

pred_diagnosis: In Shift, the loop writes the heap (arr[i]), so the loop inherits the method's modifies clause. That clause includes this`top. The loop invariants say nothing about top, so after the loop Dafny treats top as arbitrary. The invariants together with the exit condition therefore do not let Dafny conclude, after `top := top - 1`, that top == old(top) - 1, top >= -1 or top < capacity. That is why `ensures Valid()` and `ensures top == old(top) - 1` fail. The counterexamples show the loop forgetting the entry value of top. capacity and the arr reference are outside the frame and stay known; only top is lost.

The bounds invariant in FindWinner was weakened to `0 <= s <= n <= (|a|) + 1`. With n allowed to reach |a|+1, the next three invariants are no longer well-formed at the loop head. They call Count(a, s, |a|, K) and Count(a, s, n, k), and Count requires s <= t <= |a|. From the bounds invariant Dafny can only derive n <= |a|+1, and hence s <= |a|+1. So it cannot prove the preconditions s <= |a| (line 88) and n <= |a| (lines 89 and 90). The loop actually keeps n <= |a|, because the guard is n < |a| and each iteration adds 1 to n. So the tight bound is inductive and is the intended invariant.

The innermost loop `while (c != a)` in Determinant has no loop invariant. Inside the loop body Dafny therefore knows nothing about c beyond c != a. It cannot show that the second index c-1 of X[b-1,c-1] lies in [0, X.Length1), which is the 'index 1 out of range' error. It also cannot find a decreases measure (c - a) that is bounded below, which is the termination error on the loop. An invariant bounding c between a and M is needed. It holds on entry, since c == M and a <= M. It is preserved, because c != a and a <= c give a < c, so c-1 still satisfies a <= c-1 <= M. It also makes c-1 a valid index (0 <= a-1 < c-1 < M) and lets Dafny infer decreases c - a.

The loop in sumOdds has only the invariant sum == (i + 1) * (i + 1). It has no bound on i. After the loop Dafny knows just the invariant and !(i < n-1), which gives i >= n-1 but not i == n-1. So it cannot conclude sum == n * n at the assert on line 16. The counterexample (n = 514, i = 0 on entry) reflects that i is left unconstrained after the loop. An upper-bound invariant on i is needed so that the exit condition forces i == n-1.

The bound invariant `0 <= i <= (size) + 1` is off by one. It allows i == size + 1, so the slices `ret[..i]` and `a[l..(l + i)]` in the next invariant may exceed ret.Length (== size) and possibly a.Length. Dafny therefore reports the two upper-bound well-formedness errors at line 19. For the same reason, at loop exit `!(i < size)` together with `i <= size + 1` does not force i == size. So `ret[..i] == a[l..l+i]` cannot be turned into `ret[..] == a[l..r]`, and the postcondition fails.

The invariants only describe the prefix b[0..next): b's in [0,white), a's in [white,next), plus pairwise ordering facts restricted to indices below next. Nothing is said about the suffix b[blue..|b|), where the loop puts every 'd' it swaps out. When the loop exits with next == blue, Dafny knows nothing about the contents or relative order of positions >= blue. So it cannot conclude sortedbad(b), whose quantifiers range over the whole string, for example that every 'b' comes before every 'd'. The invariants are maintained, but together with the exit condition they are too weak to imply the postcondition. An invariant fixing the suffix as all 'd's is missing.
pred_repair: invariant forall i :: blue <= i < |b| ==> b[i] == 'd';

pred_diagnosis: The loop invariants never bound i above by row (intervals.Length0). This causes two failures. First, the invariant 'intervals[0, 1] <= end <= intervals[i - 1, 1]' is not well-formed, because i - 1 may be outside 0..Length0-1, which gives the index-out-of-range error. Second, after the loop Dafny knows only '1 <= count <= i && !(i < row)'. That says nothing about count <= row, so the returned value row - count cannot be shown to be >= 0, and the postcondition 'count >= 0' fails on the return path. Adding the upper bound i <= row makes the array access well-formed. At exit it also gives i == row, so count <= row and row - count >= 0.

In PositiveSet.find the loop has no bounds invariant on i. The Set and GrowingSet versions have `invariant 0 <= i <= nelems`, but this one does not. At the loop head Dafny treats i as arbitrary. So in `forall j :: 0 <= j < i ==> x != store[j]`, j can reach values at or beyond nelems, and therefore at or beyond store.Length. That makes `store[j]` an out-of-range access (the counterexample has nelems = store.Length = 610). Without a bound on i, the invariant cannot be shown well-formed or re-established across iterations, and the indexing inside it fails.

The loop in query has no invariant bounding ind. As a result, the invariant 'res == sum(a, i, j) - sum(a, i, ind+1)' is not well-formed: sum requires 0 <= i <= ind+1 <= a.Length, and nothing guarantees i <= ind+1 (or ind+1 <= a.Length) after an iteration. Also, on exit Dafny only knows !(ind >= i), i.e. ind < i. It cannot conclude ind == i-1, so sum(a, i, ind+1) cannot be reduced to sum(a, i, i) == 0 and the postcondition res == sum(a, i, j) does not follow. A bounds invariant on ind, placed before the res invariant, fixes both the well-formedness and the exit (bridge) step.

The second loop invariant in Flip only covers index pairs with 0 <= i <= j < N - 1. It says nothing about the last row and column, j == N-1. The weakened invariant is still established and preserved, but at exit (a == N) it only describes the elements with indices below N-1.
